explanation: Assumption: A generic lambda parameter defined as `auto x` automatically handles efficient passing (copy vs. move) to downstream functions. Reality: Any named parameter `x` inside the lambda body is treated as an lvalue, regardless of whether the original caller passed an rvalue. Why It Fails: This lvalue decay prevents the selection of move semantics (rvalue reference overloads) in downstream functions, leading to unnecessary copying. To correctly implement perfect forwarding within a generic lambda, the parameter must be declared as a universal reference (`auto&&`) and subsequently passed using `std::forward<DeclType>(x)` (where `DeclType` is the deduced type of the parameter, often found via `decltype(x)`).
practical_example: A generic lambda is written to act as a wrapper, accepting any argument type and forwarding it to a resource-intensive function (e.g., a network sender). If the lambda fails to use `auto&&` and `std::forward`, temporary objects passed to the lambda are copied instead of moved into the sender's buffer, incurring significant performance penalties.
keywords: Generic lambda perfect forwarding, lambda lvalue decay, auto&& lambda, std::forward lambda argument
chapter: Item 33: Use decltype on auto&& parameters to std::forward them
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
